newsitem.title: USA: SBC AT&T deal seen addressing antitrust issue.
newsitem.headline: SBC AT&T deal seen addressing antitrust issue.

text.p: A potential merger of SBC Comunications Inc. and AT&T Corp. would likely include a detailed plan to open SBC's local markets to competitors in an attempt to alleviate antitrust concerns.
The two companies also would be expected to defend a union against antitrust concerns by arguing that telecommunications is an increasingly competitive business with strong players around the globe.

A source involved in merger talks between the two companies said that SBC officials are well aware that a potential merger of the two telecommunications giants would generate antitrust issues in the seven states in which the regional Bell operates.
"They would certainly feel that they have got to solve that issue to the satisfaction of regulators," said the source who declined to be identified.

"The only places you could argue that there would be a reduction of competition is in the seven states where SBC has local service. Other than that, the two just don't overlap," he said, adding that if the companies strike a deal, "they are going to offer a comprehensive plan that would make this deal pro-competitive," the source said.

So far, both companies have refused to publicly comment on the talks first reported last week by the Wall Street Journal. The source said the two companies are entrenched in talks about a possible combination, but a deal is not imminent.

A union of SBC and AT&T would bring together a mighty provider of local service with a long distance powerhouse in the first such transaction since the 1984 federal order that broke apart the Bell monopoly by creating regional Bells and prohibiting AT&T from entering local markets.

According to the Telecommunications Act of 1996, regional Bell companies may enter long-distance markets if they open up their own local markets to competition. But long distance companies like AT&T have continually complained that the regional Bells, including SBC, are dragging their feet.

Experts across Wall Street and the telecommunications industry last week said that any potential merger of the local and long-distance giants would generate intense scrutiny from local and federal regulators.

John Collins, who specialises in antitrust issues at law firm Dewey Ballantine, said a union of the two companies does not indicate the formation of a giant company that will take control of the nation's telecommunications industry.
"They are putting together a couple of pieces," he said.

Meanwhile, the globalization argument is one that has been increasingly used in other unions of major companies, including the proposed merger of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp., and a massive proposed alliance between American Airlines and British Airways Plc.

The telecommunications industry has been packed with large transactons, including the proposed unions of regional Bells NYNEX and Bell Atlantic Corp. ; a proposed merger of British Telecommunications Inc. and MCI Communications Corp. and stakes taken in Sprint Corp. by the national telecommunications companies of France and Germany.

However, a union of AT&T with SBC would be the first major transaction that would combine a local service and a long distance company, thereby creating scepticism abou the likely outcome of a proposed transaction.
"I think it's going to be very difficult for the Department of Justice to sign off on this merger," said one Wall Street analyst.
